1:
How Mordecai came by the news is answered plainly, then piously. John Gill (reformed) allows that he learned it by common fame or on sight of the edicts published in Shushan, though he records that the Jews think it was made known supernaturally, the former Targum saying by Elijah and the latter by the Holy Ghost. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) says he gave every demonstration of poignant and oppressive grief, and reports from the Greek that he protested aloud that a people were going to be destroyed who had done no evil. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) sees deliberate publicity in it: he not only vented his grief but proclaimed it, that all might notice he was not ashamed to own himself a fellow-sufferer with the Jews, however despicable Haman’s faction now made them. It was nobly done, Henry adds, to espouse publicly a cause he knew to be righteous when it seemed a sinking one; and Mordecai laid it to heart more than any because Haman’s spite was against him primarily.

Two schools notice the same absence. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) observes that the sorrow of Mordecai and of the Jews alike is described by external manifestations solely: rending of garments, sackcloth and ashes, fasting and weeping and wailing, with nothing said of prayer to the God of Israel. Daniel and Ezra and Nehemiah, he points out, were Jews who like these submitted to the rule of the alien, but who, unlike them, besought their God when danger threatened, and not in vain. Clarke makes it an exclamation: how astonishing that in all this there is not the slightest intimation given of praying to God.

On the gate the voices divide between construction and reason. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) take the king’s gate to be the open space before the entrance to the royal palace, and read the prohibition as an impersonal construction: there is no entering, none may enter. Ellicott supplies the motive, that nothing sad or ill-omened might meet the monarch’s gaze, as though by shutting his eyes to sorrow or sickness or death he might suppose he was evading them. Henry draws out the cost: the arbitrary power of these kings often set many a mourning, yet none might come near in mourning dress, because the king was not willing to hear such complaints; and to forbid sackcloth to enter, unless they could forbid sickness and trouble and death to enter, was a jest.

The mourning in the provinces is measured by Keil and Delitzsch in grammar and by Henry in self-denial. The former read the clause naming the place as an adverbial accusative in apposition, so that the sense is: in every place the king’s word and decree reached, a great mourning arose among the Jews; and where the text says sackcloth and ashes were spread for many, the meaning is that many sat in hairy garments upon the earth where ashes had been spread, as the prophet Isaiah pictures the chosen fast. Henry counts the cost in ordinary comforts: they denied themselves their tables, mingling tears with their drink, and their beds at night, lying in sackcloth and ashes.

Why Esther sent clothes draws two readings and a third thought. Clarke supposes she thought he must somehow have been spoiled of his raiment, and sent him clothing. Keil and Delitzsch go further, that it was evidently to enable him to enter the palace and give her the particulars, and they note that the word for her distress is an intensive form, a convulsive grief. Henry takes the refusal as itself a message: she sent the oil of joy for mourning and the garments of praise for the spirit of heaviness, but because he would make her sensible of the greatness of his grief, and so of its cause, he was as one that refused to be comforted.
5:
The messenger gets more attention than the message, and the reason is the harem. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) explains that so strictly did the laws of Persia confine the king’s wives that it was not possible for Mordecai to have a conference with Esther at all; the whole exchange had therefore to be carried by Hatach, whom the king had appointed to attend her, and who seems to have been one she could confide in. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) reads that appointment less charitably: the eunuch was set to wait upon her partly, as is still the case in the East, to serve her, and partly to observe her conduct, for no despot is exempt from a twofold torture, jealousy and suspicion. John Gill (reformed) notes that the Targum makes this officer Daniel, but thinks it not likely Daniel lived so long, and settles for the double fact that the king trusted him with the queen’s care and that she herself had a high opinion of him.

What she asked, and where, is handled between grammar and sympathy. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) render her commission with the bluntness of the Hebrew, to learn what this and why this, that is, the meaning and the cause of his thus going about in mourning; and they place the interview in the open place of the city before the king’s gate. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) adds only that the word rendered street means the square or wide open place. Gill observes that Mordecai was there in a public manner, expressing his grief. Henry turns her enquiry into a rule: to enquire after news, that we may know the better how to direct our griefs and joys, our prayers and praises, well becomes all that love Sion, for if we must weep with those that weep, we must know why they weep.

On what Mordecai reported, the voices differ over the heart of it. Keil and Delitzsch fix on the money: Mordecai told the amount Haman had promised to weigh to the king’s treasures, that is, to pay into the royal treasury, for leave to destroy the Jews; the term is properly a determined and accurate statement, hence a sum, and the promise is mentioned emphatically as the chief point of the report. Gill fixes on the grievance behind it, that for refusing to reverence Haman he was incensed against Mordecai, and against all the Jews for his sake, and had vowed revenge and formed a scheme for their ruin; and he explains how the copy came to hand, the decree having been published in the city, so Mordecai had sight of it and transcribed it. Henry fixes on what the copy was for: she must see the danger she and her people were in.

The charge, and a speech that may not belong to it, close the embassy. Henry gives the charge as Mordecai pressed it, that if she had any respect for him or kindness for the Jewish nation she should appear now on their behalf, rectify the misinformations by which the king had been imposed upon, and set the matter in a true light, not doubting that he would then vacate the decree. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same charge through the construction, taking the infinitives forward rather than back, with Bertheau, so that what must be supplied is that Mordecai commissioned Hatach to declare the matter to Esther and command her to go in unto the king. Clarke reports that the Greek inserts here a plea in Mordecai’s own mouth, bidding her remember the time of her low estate and how she had been nourished and carried in his arms, and pray to the Lord and plead with the king for deliverance from death; but there is not a word of this, he observes, in the Hebrew, the Syriac, or the Vulgate.
10:
The law Esther pleads is described four ways, one charitably. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) traces it to pretension: the Persian sovereigns affected the highest degree of majesty, even to assuming Divine honours, so that none dared appear unveiled before them without hazarding life, and into the inner chamber of the harem none entered but the king and the woman he had chosen to call thither. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) allows a reason of state, that it was decreed to maintain the majesty and the safety of the king’s person, but adds a second cause that is no reason of state, the contrivance of the greater officers, that few might have access to the king but themselves and their friends. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) keeps to the Hebrew: literally, one is his law, one unvarying rule for such. John Gill (reformed) notices who knew it: not the courtiers only but the meanest of the king’s subjects, there being scarce a person in the empire to whom it was unknown, which shows how notorious it was.

Ellicott supports the sceptre from the monuments, then turns it against the throne. In the Persian royal representations at Persepolis, he reports, the monarch always holds a long staff or sceptre in his right hand; and he sets the contrast forcibly, between this self-styled king of kings, to enter whose presence even as a suppliant was to risk death, and the King of Kings who himself instructs man to say, let us go into his tabernacle and fall low on our knees before his footstool. On the thirty days both read her position as weak. Wesley says the lapse gave her just cause to fear the king’s affections were alienated, and that neither her person nor petition would be acceptable. Clarke suspects a hand in it, and cannot but think Haman the cause, having endeavoured to draw the king’s attention from the queen so that his affection might be lessened.

Mordecai’s reply is read as confident, then weighed. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) press the first clause, that to be saved in the king’s house above all the Jews means saved alone of all the Jews, and render the rest without softening: recovery and deliverance will arise from another place, but thou and thy father’s house shall be destroyed; who knows if thou hast attained to royalty for a time such as this. Ellicott translates the hope more narrowly, enlargement being literally a breathing-space, and thinks Mordecai speaks with studied reserve, not explaining himself, though we may suppose he means Divine help in this extremity. But he will not take the saying for proof of the man’s faith: had his faith been like that of many of his countrymen, he would not have been in Persia at all, but with the struggling band in the homeland.

On the famous question two schools converge, and Ellicott keeps back. Clarke expands it into a challenge: is it likely Divine providence would have so distinguished her, raising her from abject obscurity, merely for her own sake? Must it not have been on some public account, and has he not put her where she may counteract the most ruinous purpose ever formed? He makes it general: no human being lacks some particular station, by an especial providence and at some particular time, in which he may be of essential service to his neighbour. Wesley draws the lesson shortly: we should consider for what end God has put us where we are, and when an opportunity offers of serving God and our generation, take care not to let it slip. Ellicott finds instead in the whole tone of the conversation a lack of nobler feeling, no suggestion of turning for aid to God, and thinks that when God did carry out his purpose the deliverance came indirectly, without special blessing on the human instruments.
15:
What Esther ordered takes a practical shape and a cautious one. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) reads the command to fast as a command to fast and pray, as they were used to do: they were to leave off their common dinners by day and suppers at night, and eat no more than mere necessity required, that so they might give themselves to constant and fervent prayer. The maidens, he adds, were those she had chosen to attend her person, doubtless Jews or proselytes. John Gill (reformed) sees a precaution in the wording: they were gathered to be acquainted with what follows, not to continue in a body together, which might cause suspicion of an ill design. He will not take the numbers he finds, either: the latter Targum reports twelve thousand chosen priests in the city, which must be an exaggeration, since it can hardly be thought there were so many Jews there in all.

The three days are reckoned out by Wesley with care, because the queen goes in on the third. He takes the qualification to belong to the time rather than the thing, and observes that the fast began at evening, so she might continue it three whole nights, two whole days, and the greatest part of the third, a part of a day being reputed a day in the account of scripture and of other authors. She might have fasted all that day too, since it is probable she went not to the king till he had dined, hoping to find him in the mildest humour.

Where Wesley supplies the prayer, Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) refuses to. What a strange thing, he writes, that still we hear nothing of prayer, nor of God; and asked on what ground we can account for this total silence, he answers that he does not know. She could not suppose there was any charm in fasting, in sackcloth garments, in lying on the ground; and if these were not done to turn away the displeasure of God, which seemed now to have unchained their enemies, what were they done for? Of the resolve itself he is warmer: if she lose her life in this attempt to save her people, she will lose it cheerfully, seeing it her duty and resolved, come what will, to do it. Even here he adds a reservation, that she must have depended much on the efficacy of the humiliations she prescribed.

The last verse is read plainly by one voice and as a difficulty by another. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) take it simply, that Mordecai went from the place before the court of the king to do what the queen had commanded. Gill notes that the verb used has sometimes the sense of passing over or transgressing, and reports that Jarchi took it so, of Mordecai transgressing the command by fasting on a festival: the letter having been written on the thirteenth of Nisan, the next day was the passover, on which he supposes the fast began, so that the three days fell within the feast of unleavened bread, as the Targum also has it.
